title: Natural numbers and integers
competency: Tell natural numbers from integers and describe how the two sets are related.

keywords.def: A collection of well-defined, distinct objects. No object appears twice.
A counting number: 1, 2, 3, … The set is written ℕ.
A whole number or its negative: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … The set is written ℤ.

en.text: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. We write this set as ℕ. Integers are the natural numbers, zero, and their negatives. We write this set as ℤ. Every natural number is an integer. But not every integer is a natural number.

am.text: የተፈጥሮ ቁጥሮች የመቁጠሪያ ቁጥሮች ናቸው፤ 1፣ 2፣ 3 እና የመሳሰሉት። ይህን ስብስብ ℕ ብለን እንጽፋለን። ኢንቲጀሮች የተፈጥሮ ቁጥሮች፣ ዜሮ እና አሉታዊዎቻቸው ናቸው። ይህን ስብስብ ℤ ብለን እንጽፋለን። ማንኛውም የተፈጥሮ ቁጥር ኢንቲጀር ነው፤ ግን ማንኛውም ኢንቲጀር የተፈጥሮ ቁጥር አይደለም።

screens.title: Counting sheep
screens.text: Kebede counts his sheep: 1, 2, 3, … He never counts 0 sheep or −25 sheep.
screens.ask: Which of 6, 0 and −25 could be a count of sheep?
screens.after:
Only 6. You can count 6 sheep.
Counting starts at 1, so 0 is not a count.
You cannot have −25 sheep, so negatives are not counts.
Read on to name these numbers.

screens.title: Sets of numbers
paras: Recall that a set is a collection of well-defined, distinct objects.
Distinct means no object appears twice.
In Grade 7 you met two sets of numbers.
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …} is the set of natural numbers.
ℤ = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …} is the set of integers.

screens.title: ℕ sits inside ℤ
screens.ask: Tap a circle. Then tap each number to see its sets.
rings: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … Zero and the negatives are here too.
numbers: A counting number. It is in ℕ, so it is in ℤ too.
0 is an integer. It is not a counting number.
A negative integer. It is not natural.
A counting number, so it is in both sets.

screens.title: Name the sets
defs: A collection of well-defined, distinct objects. No object appears twice.
A counting number: 1, 2, 3, … The set is ℕ.
A whole number or its negative: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … The set is ℤ.

screens.title: Integer, not natural
screens.text: Which number is an integer but NOT a natural number?
screens.why:
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …} starts at 1.
ℤ = {…, −1, 0, 1, …} also holds 0 and the negatives.
7, 100 and 1 are counting numbers, so they are in both sets.
0 is in ℤ but not in ℕ. So the answer is 0.
screens.clue: Where does the list for ℕ start?

screens.title: How ℕ and ℤ are related
paras: Every natural number is an integer. We write ℕ ⊆ ℤ.
Not every integer is a natural number. 5 is natural, but −5 is not.
Picture a circle for ℕ drawn inside a bigger circle for ℤ.
screens.note: The book shows this diagram as Figure 1.2 in lesson 1.2.

screens.title: Sort the numbers
screens.text: Sort into sets: put each number in the right group.
items: ℕ starts at 1, so 0 is not natural.
Negative numbers are not in ℕ.
Negative numbers are not in ℕ.
screens.why:
Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …
6 and 12 are counting numbers: natural.
0 is not a counting number: an integer only.
−25 and −1 are negative: integers only.
screens.clue: Ask: could I count this many objects?

screens.title: Always, sometimes or never?
screens.text: Natural numbers: is the sentence "−7 is a natural number" always, sometimes or never true?
screens.why:
Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, … All are positive.
−7 is negative.
So −7 is never in ℕ. Never true.
("Sometimes" would need −7 to be natural in some cases, but −7 is one fixed number.)
screens.clue: Look at where the list for ℕ starts.

screens.title: True or false?
screens.text: Natural numbers and integers: every integer is a natural number.
screens.why:
Test one integer that is not positive.
−5 is an integer, but not a counting number.
0 is an integer, but ℕ starts at 1.
So not every integer is natural. False.
(The opposite is true: every natural number is an integer.)

screens.title: Lift buttons
screens.text: A lift in an Addis Ababa building has buttons −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
screens.ask: Count the natural numbers: ___ of these buttons show natural numbers.
screens.why:
The buttons are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Cross out the negatives −2 and −1.
Cross out 0: ℕ starts at 1.
Left: 1, 2, 3, 4.
So 4 buttons show natural numbers.
screens.clue: Cross out 0 and the negatives. Count what is left.
screens.worked: Cross out −2, −1 and 0. Left: 1, 2, 3, 4. That is 4 buttons.

items.text: Natural numbers: which of 6, 0 and −25 are natural numbers?
items.why:
Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …
6 is a counting number: natural.
0 is not: ℕ starts at 1.
−25 is negative: not natural.
So 6 only. (All three are integers.)
items.clue: Natural numbers are the counting numbers.

items.text: Sets of numbers: "Natural numbers are integers." Always, sometimes or never true?
items.why:
ℤ = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
Every counting number 1, 2, 3, … is in this list.
So every natural number is an integer: ℕ ⊆ ℤ.
Always true.

items.text: Sets of numbers: "Integers are natural numbers." Always, sometimes or never true?
items.why:
Try a positive integer: 5 is natural. So it can be true.
Try a negative integer: −5 is not natural.
Try 0: it is not natural either.
It is true for some integers only. Sometimes true.
items.clue: Try one positive and one negative integer.

items.text: Natural numbers: "−7 is a natural number." Always, sometimes or never true?
items.why:
Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3, …
They are never negative.
−7 is negative, so it is not natural.
Never true.

items.ask: Count the natural numbers: ___ of these numbers are natural numbers.
items.why:
Natural numbers are positive counting numbers.
Leave out 0 and the negatives −11, −46, −19.
Left: 8, 23, 534, 100.
That is 4 natural numbers. (All eight are integers.)

items.ask: Integers in order: the last integer before one thousand is ___.
items.why:
Integers go up in steps of 1.
The integer just before 1,000 is 1,000 − 1.
1,000 − 1 = 999.
So the answer is 999.

items.text: Closure: for any natural numbers n₁ and n₂, n₁ + n₂ is always a natural number.
items.why:
Take two counting numbers, for example 3 and 5.
3 + 5 = 8, a counting number.
Adding two positive numbers always gives a bigger positive number.
It can never be 0 or negative.
So ℕ is closed under addition. True.
items.clue: Add two counting numbers. Can you get 0 or a negative?

items.text: Closure: for any natural numbers n₁ and n₂, n₁ − n₂ is always a natural number.
items.why:
Try a small number minus a bigger one.
3 − 5 = −2, which is not natural.
Also 4 − 4 = 0, which is not natural.
One example is enough to show "always" is wrong.
So ℕ is not closed under subtraction. False.
items.clue: Try a small number minus a bigger one.

items.text: Triangle with natural-number sides: the perimeter is 10. Which side lengths are possible?
items.why:
The sides add to 10.
In a triangle, the two short sides must add to more than the long side.
So the longest side is less than half of 10: at most 4.
With longest side 4: 2, 4, 4 and 3, 3, 4 work.
With longest side 3 or less, the sum is at most 9.
So the answer is 2, 4, 4 or 3, 3, 4. (2, 3, 5 fails: 2 + 3 = 5 is not more than 5.)
items.clue: In a triangle, the two short sides must add to more than the long side.

items.text: m and n are positive integers with m + n < 10.
items.ask: Count the products: mn can take ___ different values.
items.why:
m + n < 10, so m + n is at most 9.
m = 1: n = 1 to 8 gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.
m = 2: n = 1 to 7 adds 10, 12, 14.
m = 3: n = 1 to 6 adds 9, 15, 18.
m = 4: n = 1 to 5 adds 16, 20. Larger m gives no new products.
Count: 8 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 16 different values.
items.clue: List the products for m = 1, then m = 2, and so on. Count each value once.
items.worked: m = 1 gives 1–8. m = 2 adds 10, 12, 14. m = 3 adds 9, 15, 18. m = 4 adds 16, 20. Total 16.

test.text: Sets of numbers: which set contains 0?
test.why:
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …} starts at 1, so 0 is not in ℕ.
ℤ = {…, −1, 0, 1, …} includes 0.
So 0 is in ℤ only.

test.text: Set symbols: ℕ ⊆ ℤ means every natural number is an integer.
test.why:
⊆ means "is a subset of".
ℕ ⊆ ℤ says every element of ℕ is also in ℤ.
1, 2, 3, … all appear in ℤ.
So the sentence is true.

test.ask: Natural numbers: the smallest natural number is ___.
test.why:
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}.
The list starts at 1.
0 is not a natural number.
So the smallest natural number is 1.
